paragraphs: Transformer designs often inherit familiar choices about width and depth, such as a hidden size of 768 and 12 layers. This paper asks whether those defaults suit different training objectives equally well. Its central finding is that the best configuration depends closely on what the model is trained to do.

The authors compare classification training with masked autoencoder training and find that the latter better alleviates over-smoothing in deep transformers. Over-smoothing concerns representations becoming too similar as processing proceeds through layers. This observation motivates Bamboo: using more layers with narrower representations when training with a masked autoencoder objective.

The reported results show that this configuration change can improve both vision and language models. The redesigned Base-level vision transformer reaches 84.2% ImageNet top-1 accuracy, with a reported 0.9% improvement over MAE. On eight GLUE datasets, the redesigned language model exceeds default BERT by 1.1 points on average. These findings support choosing transformer shape together with the training objective.
icml-2023-a-study-on-transformer-configu.tldr: Bamboo uses deeper, narrower transformers to improve results when the training objective supports effective learning at greater depth.

paragraphs: Standard neural networks usually apply a fixed kind and amount of computation regardless of how difficult an example is. AdaTape introduces flexibility by allowing the input sequence itself to change. This gives the network a way to adapt the information it processes, rather than requiring every example to use an identical sequence structure.

The method equips an architecture with a dynamic read-and-write tape built from additional tape tokens. These tokens come from a bank that can be learned during training or constructed from the input data. The proposed Adaptive Tape Reading algorithm controls both which content enters the sequence and how long that sequence becomes.

Experiments on image recognition show that AdaTape can improve performance while maintaining computational cost. The result supports adaptive sequence construction as a useful way to allocate computation without simply increasing the overall budget. Its contribution is therefore both an architecture mechanism and an algorithm for making sequence content and length responsive to the example being processed.
icml-2023-adaptive-computation-with-elas.tldr: AdaTape adapts input sequence content and length to improve image recognition performance at maintained computational cost.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how well a target decision policy would perform using observations collected under another policy. A major obstacle arises when unmeasured variables affect both the actions taken and their rewards or subsequent states. In that situation, observed associations can misrepresent the consequences of following the target policy.

This paper develops an instrumental-variable approach to that problem in sequential decision making. The authors show that instrumental variables can identify the target policy's value even in an infinite-horizon setting, where decisions and their consequences continue over time. This extends the role of instrumental variables beyond evaluating a single decision.

The work also proposes several estimators for policy value and illustrates their effectiveness through simulations and analysis of data from a short-video platform. Its theoretical contribution concerns consistent evaluation despite unmeasured confounding within the instrumental-variable framework. Its practical contribution is to turn that identification result into estimators that can be applied to observational decision data.
icml-2023-an-instrumental-variable-appro.tldr: An instrumental-variable framework enables consistent evaluation of policies from confounded sequential observational data.

paragraphs: Unsupervised skill discovery seeks to give a reinforcement learning agent diverse behaviors without supplying external rewards. Earlier approaches often maximize mutual information between states and skills, encouraging states to reveal which skill is active. The authors argue that this objective can favor simple, static skills and restrict exploration.

Their alternative contrasts behaviors directly. It encourages behaviors produced by the same skill to resemble one another while making behaviors from different skills distinct. Under mild assumptions, the objective maximizes mutual information between different behaviors associated with the same skill. That quantity upper-bounds the earlier state-and-skill mutual-information objective.

The method also implicitly increases state entropy, supporting broader coverage of the environment. In challenging mazes and continuous control tasks, it produces diverse skills that reach farther through the environment and delivers competitive downstream performance against state-of-the-art methods. Together, the theoretical relationship and experiments support using behavioral diversity to learn skills that do more than remain distinguishable at isolated states.
icml-2023-behavior-contrastive-learning-.tldr: Contrasting behaviors helps agents discover diverse, far-reaching skills without external rewards.

paragraphs: Coarse-grained protein simulations gain speed by representing groups of atoms as single beads. Backmapping reconstructs the atom-level detail that this simplification removes. The challenge is to do so quickly while producing plausible geometry and transferring between proteins, rather than requiring a reconstruction method tailored to each individual protein.

The proposed generative method combines several design choices to address these requirements. It represents structures through internal coordinates, uses an equivariant encoder and prior, and trains with a custom loss that addresses local structure, global structure, and physical constraints. Expert-curated protein data outside equilibrium supplies another part of the training approach.

These choices target problems seen in earlier methods, including steric clashes, implausible torsion angles, and poor transfer between proteins. The authors report progress toward fast, reliable, transferable backmapping. They frame the results as paving the way for ready-to-use reconstruction of arbitrary proteins, rather than establishing that unrestricted generality as an already completed outcome.
icml-2023-chemically-transferable-genera.tldr: A generative backmapping method combines structural representations, physical constraints, and curated data to improve reliability and transfer between proteins.

paragraphs: This paper studies training across workers connected through a decentralized network, where different workers hold different data distributions. The optimization problems are nonconvex and composite, requiring more than a plain gradient update. The goal is to handle this heterogeneity while keeping both data use per update and communication costs manageable.

The authors introduce DProxSGT, a proximal stochastic method with gradient tracking, and a compressed version that reduces the information exchanged between workers. Both use only a constant number of samples per worker for each proximal update. Gradient tracking provides the mechanism for handling differences in the data held across the network.

Under a smoothness condition on the expected loss, without requiring that condition for every sample loss, the methods achieve optimal sample complexity for reaching a near-stationary point. This is a stationarity guarantee, not a global-optimum claim. Neural-network experiments report better generalization than large-batch and momentum variance-reduction methods, alongside evidence that gradient tracking handles heterogeneous data.
icml-2023-compressed-decentralized-proxi.tldr: Decentralized gradient tracking with optional communication compression supports small-sample updates and provable convergence for heterogeneous nonconvex training.

paragraphs: Multimodal encoders learn from both images and language, often using large unlabeled datasets. This creates an opportunity for data poisoning: altering training examples to induce unwanted model behavior. The paper investigates vulnerabilities in both modalities, extending the focus beyond attacks that modify only the visual side of training.

The authors propose three types of poisoning attacks to examine whether language is vulnerable and how poisoning effects differ across modalities. Evaluations across datasets and model architectures show substantial attack performance while preserving model utility in both vision and language. This means ordinary usefulness can coexist with the malicious behaviors induced by poisoned training data.

The paper also introduces defenses applied before training and after training. Both empirically reduce attack performance while preserving utility. The findings establish that poisoning is a concern across modalities and that its effect depends on the modality involved. The reported defenses mitigate the tested attacks; the results do not amount to a claim that all poisoning vulnerabilities are removed.
icml-2023-data-poisoning-attacks-against.tldr: Multimodal encoders are vulnerable to poisoning across image and language data, while proposed defenses reduce tested attacks without sacrificing utility.

paragraphs: Panoramic depth completion must contend with geometry that standard pixelwise losses do not capture. Treating every pixel equally overlooks distortion that changes with latitude in an equirectangular panorama. The task also has elevated uncertainty near textures and edges, where depth predictions can be less accurate than in smoother regions.

The proposed distortion and uncertainty aware loss addresses these issues through two components. Its distortion component uses the projection's coordinate transformation to assign unequal pixel importance according to latitude. Its uncertainty component uses a Bayesian deep learning framework to account for uncertainty in depth completion, particularly around non-smooth regions.

A further constraint encourages multiple uncertainty maps for the same panorama to agree. The authors report that this improves uncertainty estimation and makes it robust to feature deformation. Extensive experiments show improvements over standard loss functions and state-of-the-art performance. The contribution is a training objective that reflects both panoramic projection geometry and spatial differences in prediction uncertainty.
icml-2023-distortion-and-uncertainty-awa.tldr: A loss combining projection-aware pixel weighting and consistent uncertainty estimation improves panoramic depth completion.

paragraphs: In multiplayer online games, participants repeatedly make decisions while interacting with one another. This paper considers strongly monotone games, a structured class with favorable theoretical properties, when the environment changes over time. The challenge is to obtain strong learning guarantees despite those changes, rather than assuming a fixed game throughout.

The authors propose a decentralized online algorithm that improves previously available guarantees for this setting. It obtains fast rates matching the best time-invariant guarantee without needing prior knowledge of environmental non-stationarity. That lack of advance knowledge matters because the algorithm must accommodate change without being told beforehand how much change to expect.

The paper also extends the RVU property using smoothness and derives a series of problem-dependent bounds for faster rates. These results likewise match the best time-invariant bound described in the abstract. The contribution combines techniques from non-stationary and universal online learning, with guarantees specifically developed for time-varying strongly monotone games rather than arbitrary multiplayer interactions.
icml-2023-fast-rates-in-time-varying-str.tldr: A decentralized algorithm achieves fast theoretical rates in time-varying strongly monotone games without knowing the amount of environmental change.

paragraphs: Adversarial training aims to make neural networks resist small input changes that can mislead predictions while remaining imperceptible to people. This paper focuses on how training treats examples with different levels of vulnerability. Its main idea is to place greater regularization on examples that are more susceptible to adversarial attacks.

The proposed algorithm strengthens that treatment of vulnerable data relative to existing regularization methods. The authors also derive a new upper bound on robust risk and show that their algorithm can be interpreted as minimizing it. This gives the training rule a theoretical motivation tied directly to controlling risk under adversarial perturbations.

Numerical experiments show simultaneous improvements in accuracy on ordinary examples and accuracy under adversarial attacks, reaching the reported state of the art. The findings suggest that directing regularization toward vulnerable samples can improve both generalization and robustness in the evaluated settings. The upper-bound interpretation explains the design, while the experiments provide the evidence for its performance benefits.
icml-2023-improving-adversarial-robustne.tldr: Applying stronger regularization to attack-vulnerable examples improves both ordinary and adversarial accuracy in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Deep equilibrium models repeatedly apply a single transformation until reaching a fixed point, instead of using a conventional stack of distinct layers. This paper argues that adversarial training should account for that iterative structure. The authors find that existing adversarial training insufficiently regulates the intermediate states encountered during the model's computation.

Those intermediate states also tend to produce high-entropy predictions, meaning that their predictions are spread across possibilities. Motivated by a relationship between dynamical-system entropy and stability, the authors propose progressively updating inputs along the neural dynamics to reduce prediction entropy. They also compute the adversarial-training loss using randomly selected intermediate states.

Together, these interventions regulate the path toward equilibrium rather than focusing only on the final prediction. Extensive experiments report substantial gains in adversarial robustness, including performance above strong deep-network baselines. The results support using the distinctive computation of equilibrium models to design robustness methods; the entropy-and-stability connection provides motivation for those interventions rather than an unconditional robustness guarantee.
icml-2023-improving-adversarial-robustne.tldr: Regulating intermediate states during equilibrium-model computation substantially improves adversarial robustness in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can benefit from information located far away in a graph. Increasing depth is one way to capture these dependencies, but it creates a scalability problem: the neighborhoods involved in computation can expand rapidly. On large graphs, this neighborhood explosion makes deeper models expensive to train and use.

LazyGNN pursues long-distance dependencies with a shallower model. The contribution is to separate the goal of capturing distant graph information from the need to make the model deeper. The authors also develop a mini-batch version and show compatibility with existing scaling techniques, including sampling methods, so those techniques can provide further acceleration.

Comprehensive experiments report superior prediction performance and scalability on large-scale benchmarks. These results suggest that the shallower approach can preserve useful distant dependencies while improving efficiency in the tested settings. The compatibility result also matters practically: LazyGNN can work alongside established methods for managing large graphs, expanding the available options for reducing the cost of graph representation learning.
icml-2023-lazygnn-large-scale-graph-neur.tldr: LazyGNN captures long-distance graph dependencies with shallower models and supports sampling-based acceleration.

paragraphs: Multimodal models can make correct predictions by relying on attributes that happen to accompany a class rather than attributes central to the class itself. These spurious relationships can undermine generalization. This paper addresses them during domain-specific fine-tuning, avoiding the cost and practical difficulty of intervening during large-scale pre-training.

The method uses the model's different modalities to detect spurious attributes and explicitly separate them from the affected class. A multimodal contrastive loss expresses the problematic relationships through language. Experiments and visualizations on CLIP show improved accuracy when the spurious attributes are absent and activation maps directed more toward the actual class when those attributes are present.

On Waterbirds, the authors report worst-group accuracy 23% higher than ERM for CLIP with a ResNet-50 backbone and 32% higher with a ViT backbone, while maintaining the same average accuracy. These findings show that fine-tuning can improve performance for poorly served groups without reducing average performance in this evaluation.
icml-2023-mitigating-spurious-correlatio.tldr: Language-guided contrastive fine-tuning reduces CLIP's reliance on spurious attributes and improves worst-group accuracy in the reported evaluation.

paragraphs: Clustering methods such as k-means and k-median must organize large collections of points into k groups. This paper develops quantum algorithms that first compress the clustering input into a coreset. The coreset preserves enough information for existing approximation algorithms to operate on a much smaller representation of the original dataset.

For n points in d dimensions, the construction uses approximately sqrt(nk) times d to the three-halves queries, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Its output size is polynomial in k, inverse approximation tolerance, and d. Running an alpha-approximation algorithm on this coreset yields a (1 + epsilon) times alpha approximation to the original clustering problem.

The construction gives quadratic speedups for various clustering approximation algorithms. The authors also prove a lower bound: even a constant-factor approximation requires at least order sqrt(nk) quantum queries. This nearly matches the construction's dependence on n and k, supporting its near-optimality in query complexity while leaving the stated dimensional and logarithmic factors visible.
icml-2023-near-optimal-quantum-coreset-c.tldr: Quantum coreset construction accelerates clustering approximation algorithms with nearly optimal dependence on dataset size and cluster count in query complexity.

paragraphs: The problem is to identify a population's most preferred item by repeatedly showing customers sets of alternatives and observing their choices. Each new display can depend on earlier feedback. The objective combines statistical confidence with efficiency: reach a reliable decision using as few customer-choice observations as possible.

Nested Elimination is an elimination-based algorithm inspired by the nested structure of an information-theoretic lower bound. It uses a new criterion for removing candidates and avoids solving complex combinatorial optimization problems. This makes the method simple to implement while retaining a theoretical basis for how efficiently it gathers evidence about the best item.

The authors provide an instance-specific, non-asymptotic bound on expected sample complexity, so the guarantee reflects the particular problem and is not limited to an eventual large-sample regime. They also establish high-order worst-case asymptotic optimality. Experiments using synthetic and real data support the theoretical findings, connecting the algorithm's simple elimination structure with its stated statistical efficiency.
icml-2023-nested-elimination-a-simple-al.tldr: Nested Elimination identifies the most preferred item from adaptive choice feedback with a simple algorithm and strong sample-complexity guarantees.

paragraphs: Survival analysis predicts probability distributions over when a future event will occur. Evaluating such predictions requires judging the full uncertainty estimate, rather than only a single predicted time. This paper studies scoring rules for that purpose, connecting survival analysis with the theory of proper evaluation of probabilistic forecasts.

The authors extend four major strictly proper scoring rules to survival analysis. A proper rule rewards reporting the underlying probability distribution in expectation. They prove that their extensions retain propriety under certain conditions arising from discretizing the estimated distributions. The guarantee is therefore conditional on that discretization structure, and the abstract claims propriety for the extensions rather than unrestricted strict propriety.

The paper also compares estimation performance on real datasets. Among the extended rules examined, the logarithmic-score and Brier-score versions perform best. This supplies empirical guidance alongside the theoretical analysis: the work identifies conditions supporting principled scoring and reports which extensions were most effective in the evaluated survival-estimation problems.
icml-2023-proper-scoring-rules-for-survi.tldr: Extensions of four scoring rules are proper for survival analysis under discretization-related conditions, with logarithmic and Brier extensions performing best empirically.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must learn from an existing collection of trajectories. Decision Transformers approach this through conditional sequence modeling, but lack stitching ability: combining useful portions of suboptimal trajectories into a better policy. This weakness becomes especially consequential when the dataset contains only trajectories that are themselves suboptimal.

Q-learning offers dynamic-programming machinery that does not share this limitation, although off-policy learning with function approximation can be unstable. The proposed Q-learning Decision Transformer combines the approaches through the training data. It uses dynamic-programming results to relabel return-to-go values, then trains a Decision Transformer using those revised labels.

Return-to-go labels describe the future return associated with positions in a trajectory, so changing them changes the performance information supplied during conditional training. The authors report that this combination improves performance by exploiting complementary strengths and compensating for weaknesses. The contribution is a concrete connection between value-based learning and sequence modeling, using improved return labels to address the original transformer's stitching limitation.
icml-2023-q-learning-decision-transforme.tldr: QDT uses dynamic programming to relabel trajectory returns before training a Decision Transformer, improving learning from suboptimal offline data.

paragraphs: Learning from three-dimensional graphs requires representing spatial positions alongside node attributes. Molecules provide a natural application because their graph structure comes with three-dimensional geometry. This paper proposes a quantum embedding architecture that encodes spatial structure using qubits and learns representations through a parameterized quantum circuit.

The method converts nodes' Cartesian coordinates into rotation and torsion angles, then encodes those angles into qubits. Its representation draws on the Hilbert space formed from the individual qubits' Bloch spheres. A parameterized quantum circuit supplies the trainable layers, and its output becomes the final embedding for each node.

Experiments evaluate these representations on molecular property prediction and generation of three-dimensional molecular geometries. The authors report effectiveness on QM9, a dataset containing 134,000 molecules, using very few parameters. They also identify potential for execution on a real quantum device. The stated evidence supports the embedding method on these molecular tasks, while physical-device execution is presented as a possibility.
icml-2023-quantum-3d-graph-learning-with.tldr: A quantum circuit learns compact molecular embeddings by encoding three-dimensional geometry as qubit rotation and torsion angles.

paragraphs: The ridgelet transform is a mathematical tool used to study neural networks, but its conventional numerical implementation becomes exponentially expensive as data dimension grows. This paper develops a quantum version to address that computational obstacle. The goal is to connect quantum computation with useful learning tasks involving classical neural networks.

The quantum ridgelet transform operates on a quantum state and has runtime linear in the data dimension D, compared with the stated exponential dimensional dependence of conventional classical computation. The object being transformed matters: the linear-time result concerns this quantum-state operation, which serves as a subroutine for the proposed learning application.

That application finds a sparse, trainable subnetwork inside a large, shallow, wide neural network without performing large-scale optimization of the original network. The authors present it as an efficient demonstration of the lottery ticket hypothesis in this regime. The work therefore links a faster mathematical transform to finding useful smaller networks, with the application explicitly focused on shallow, wide architectures.
icml-2023-quantum-ridgelet-transform-win.tldr: A quantum ridgelet transform runs linearly in dimension and supports finding sparse trainable subnetworks in large, shallow, wide networks.

paragraphs: Time-series explanations often identify which segments were important to a prediction. This paper instead asks for counterfactual explanations: changes to a time series that would lead to a different prediction. Its goal is a model that produces actionable explanations as part of its own prediction framework, rather than only assigning importance scores afterward.

The proposed model, Counterfactual Time Series, or CounTS, uses variational Bayesian deep learning. It incorporates counterfactual inference through time-series abduction, action, and prediction: reasoning from an observed sequence, considering an intervention, and predicting the resulting outcome. The authors also formalize the counterfactual-explanation problem and establish protocols for evaluating solutions.

Compared with state-of-the-art baselines, CounTS produces better counterfactual explanations while maintaining comparable predictive accuracy. This matters because explanation quality and prediction quality are evaluated together, rather than treating an explanation as useful regardless of the underlying predictor. The contribution combines a problem formulation, an evaluation approach, and a model designed to generate these alternative-outcome explanations directly.
icml-2023-self-interpretable-time-series.tldr: CounTS generates actionable counterfactual explanations for time-series predictions while maintaining accuracy comparable to the evaluated baselines.

paragraphs: A generated video can look convincing over a short interval yet contradict itself later. When a scene leaves view and then reappears, a model may replace it with different content. This paper targets that long-term consistency problem and introduces datasets designed to make such failures visible during evaluation.

The authors create three datasets by rendering walks through procedural mazes, Minecraft worlds, and scanned indoor scenes. They evaluate existing models on these long-range dependencies and introduce the Temporally Consistent Transformer, TECO. Its architecture compresses the input sequence into fewer embeddings, processes them with a temporal transformer, and expands them using a spatial MaskGit.

This compressed temporal representation supports modeling relationships across time before reconstructing spatial content. The reported experiments show substantial improvements in long-term consistency, reduced sampling time, and better performance across many metrics. The contribution combines an evaluation setting that requires remembering previously seen content with a generation architecture that improves that behavior in the tested environments.
icml-2023-temporally-consistent-transfor.tldr: TECO improves long-term video consistency and sampling speed, evaluated on three datasets designed around revisiting scenes.

paragraphs: How a graph is represented determines which relationships a graph neural network can process effectively. This paper develops a general framework based on parameterized decomposition and filtering. The framework brings many existing graph neural networks into a common formulation and aims to make their representation of graph information more flexible.

The authors show that spectral graph convolutions with learnable polynomial filters are constrained versions of this broader formulation. Releasing those constraints allows the model to express the desired decomposition and filtering together. This matters because flexibility then extends beyond choosing a filter within an already restricted formulation of the graph computation.

The resulting models are designed to alleviate smoothness and amplification problems in existing methods while remaining simple to implement. Experiments report significant improvements and computational efficiency across a variety of graph-learning tasks. The contribution links an explanation of restrictions in familiar spectral models with a more general formulation that produces effective practical models in the evaluated settings.
icml-2023-towards-better-graph-represent.tldr: A unified decomposition-and-filtering framework relaxes restrictions in spectral graph models and improves graph-learning performance and efficiency.

paragraphs: CREST seeks to reduce deep-network training costs by selecting the examples most useful for learning. It constructs coresets, or selected training subsets, for nonconvex models. The framework models the loss through a sequence of quadratic functions and selects a coreset within each quadratic sub-region to support convergence to a stationary point.

For stochastic training, CREST repeatedly selects multiple mini-batch coresets from larger random subsets. This aims to provide nearly unbiased gradients with low variance, supporting faster convergence. It further reduces selection overhead by identifying examples already learned and excluding them from the coreset-selection pipeline, so selection effort changes as training progresses.

Experiments across vision and language datasets report training speedups of 1.7 to 2.5 times with minimal performance loss. The tested datasets include CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet, and SNLI. Analysis of selected examples also finds that the models benefit most from subsets of increasing difficulty, connecting the efficiency gains with how useful training data changes over learning.
icml-2023-towards-sustainable-learning-c.tldr: CREST selects changing training subsets with convergence guarantees and achieves reported deep-network training speedups of 1.7 to 2.5 times.

paragraphs: Local graph clustering seeks a small cluster inside a very large graph without processing the entire graph. Existing approaches often emphasize connectivity alone, although nodes may also carry useful attributes. This paper combines those information sources so that cluster discovery reflects both graph structure and similarities between node attributes.

The proposed algorithm diffuses mass locally through the graph while accounting for structural and attribute proximity. Starting from a single seed node, it aims to recover a target cluster. The authors use high-dimensional concentration results to establish statistical performance guarantees under a contextual random graph model that includes stochastic block and planted cluster models.

The theory gives conditions under which the entire target cluster can be recovered while keeping false positives bounded. Full target recovery therefore does not mean that every returned node must belong to the target. Synthetic experiments validate the theoretical claims, and real-world graph experiments show that incorporating attributes improves local clustering. The results support combining connectivity and node information within a scalable local procedure.
icml-2023-weighted-flow-diffusion-for-lo.tldr: Local weighted diffusion combines graph structure and node attributes, with conditional recovery guarantees and improved empirical clustering.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning can produce useful representations while still overlooking meaningful distinctions. With supervision, representations of subclasses may collapse together within a broader class. Without supervision, the model may favor easy features unrelated to the class and suppress harder features that matter. This paper develops a unified theoretical framework for understanding both behaviors.

The analysis identifies the tendency of gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent to favor simpler solutions as a key factor. This simplicity bias can determine which features are learned and which distinctions disappear. The framework therefore connects representation failures at test time with the behavior of the optimization procedure used during training.

The authors present larger embedding dimensions and higher-quality data augmentations as theoretically motivated responses to feature suppression. They also explain theoretically why combining supervised and unsupervised contrastive learning can produce better representations, including with commonly used stochastic gradient methods. The contribution links feature selection, optimization bias, and several remedies within a shared explanation of contrastive representation quality.
icml-2023-which-features-are-learnt-by-c.tldr: A unified theory links contrastive feature suppression and subclass collapse to optimization's simplicity bias and motivates ways to improve representations.
